on the left, to the left
on the right, to the right
Excuse me, how do I get to the Philharmonic?
The stop is in front of the theatre.

To ask how to get somewhere and understand the answer.
To use the imperative: mergi!, mergeți!, ia-o la stânga!
To form the negative imperative: nu merge!, nu traversați!
To use prepositions of place: lângă, în fața, în spatele, între, după.
To know that “în fața”, “în spatele” are followed by the genitive (în fața teatrului).
Radu’s concert starts at seven. Mrs Pop left earlier with a friend. Nora leaves the office, but she doesn’t know exactly where the Philharmonic is. She stops a man in Union Square.
Excuse me, sir! How do I get to the Philharmonic, please?
The Philharmonic? It’s at the National Theatre, in Ștefan cel Mare Square. It’s not far.
Of course. Ten minutes. Leave the square by this street, Eroilor Boulevard. Go straight ahead to the end.
Straight ahead, to the end. And then?
Then cross at the traffic lights and turn right. You’ll see a big yellow building with columns. That’s the Opera and Theatre.
And the Philharmonic is in the theatre?
The big concerts, yes, in the Opera hall. The entrance is opposite the park. Don’t go in by the back door, that’s for the artists.
Thank you very much! Oh, one more thing: is there a florist on the way? I want to buy flowers for a friend who is playing tonight.
There’s one next to the church, on the street corner. But hurry, it closes at seven!
Thank you! Have a nice evening!
You too! And don’t get lost!
to get to, to arrive: eu ajung (I get to)
to take, to buy: “să iau” (that I take)
to play, to sing: el cântă (he plays)
In the imperative, the voice clearly falls at the end: “Mergeți drept înainte.” In a question it rises: “Merg drept înainte?”
“ia-o” and “luați-o” are read together, without a pause: “ia-o” = “yao”.
In “direct”, “drept”, “septembrie”, both consonants are heard: “drep-t”, not “drep”.
Pay attention to “ț” and “ș” at the end and in the middle of words; without them, the word changes or no longer exists.
Excuse me, where is the bus stop?
How do I get to the station?
Which bus goes to the airport?
It’s the second street on the right.
Ia-o / luați-o la stânga: “o” refers to “the direction”, “the way”. It is a fixed, very common expression.
The imperative for “tu” usually looks like the 3rd person form (el merge → mergi!) or like the “tu” form (tu vii → vino!). Each group has its tendencies:
A few imperatives are very short and irregular: “fă!” (from a face, do!), “du-te!” (go away!), “vino!” (from a veni, come!), “zi!” (from a zice, say!).
Good news: for “voi” and “dumneavoastră”, the imperative is exactly the same as the present.
Pronouns are attached AFTER the affirmative imperative, with a hyphen: “grăbiți-vă!”, “luați-o!”, “ia-o!”, “spune-mi!”.
For “tu”, the negative imperative is “nu” + the infinitive without “a”. For “voi” and “dumneavoastră” it is “nu” + the present form.
In the negative, pronouns move BEFORE the verb: “grăbește-te!” but “nu te grăbi!”.
“În fața”, “în spatele”, “în stânga”, “în dreapta” take the genitive: the noun takes the ending -ului (masculine, neuter) or -ei / -ii (feminine). We will talk more about the genitive in chapter 10.
The entrance is in front of the park.
The florist’s is behind the church.

After “lângă”, “în”, “la”, “pe” you DON’T use the article when the noun stands alone: “lângă biserică” (not “lângă biserica”). The article only appears if something follows: “lângă biserica veche” (next to the old church).
Cross the street at the traffic lights!
Affirmative: pronoun after the verb, with a hyphen.
Turn right after the traffic lights.
I want to buy flowers for a friend.
Don’t go in by the back door!
Today’s story isn’t told by Mițu. Mițu is asleep at home. Today Nora tells it.
It’s a quarter to seven. I walk quickly along Eroilor Boulevard. Straight ahead, to the end. I see the church and, next to it, the florist’s. The door is still open!

In the shop there is a small lady with glasses. “Good evening! I’d like some flowers for a musician,” I say. “What flowers does he like?” the lady asks. I don’t know. I know nothing about Radu’s favourite flowers.
“Take white roses,” says the lady. “Musicians like white roses. And they suit Enescu.” I take five white roses. They cost forty lei.
I leave the shop. I cross at the traffic lights and turn right. And I see the building: big, yellow, with white columns. It’s beautiful, especially in the evening, with the lights on.
But where is the entrance? I walk along the building. I see a small door behind the theatre. On the door it says “Artists’ entrance”. No, it’s not here.
Then I hear a voice: “Nora! Over here!” It’s Radu. He is standing in front of the door, in a black suit, with his violin in his hand.
“What are you doing here? The concert starts in five minutes!” I say. “I came out to breathe a little. I’m very nervous,” he says.
I give him the flowers. Radu looks at them and says nothing. Then he smiles. “White roses… My grandfather always brought my grandmother white roses.”
I don’t know what to say. “Go!” I say. “Go and play beautifully!” Radu goes in by the artists’ door. I run to the main entrance, in front of the park.
At seven o’clock sharp, I’m in my seat, next to Mrs Pop. She looks at me and asks quietly: “Did the flowers arrive?” “They did,” I answer. And she smiles like a satisfied teacher.
to say, to tell: el / ea spune (he / she says)
roses (flowers, usually red, white or pink)
to go out: eu ies (I go out)
“o iau la dreapta” = I turn right
to breathe: eu respir (I breathe); “să respir” (to breathe)
to enter: el intră (he goes in)

Reading text: Cluj in five minutes
Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. Tap any word to see what it means. Four questions follow at the end.
Cluj-Napoca is the second-largest city in Romania, after Bucharest.
In the centre is Union Square, with St Michael’s Church, a very tall Gothic church.
In the middle of the square is the statue of King Matthias Corvinus, on horseback.
From here, Eroilor Boulevard leads to Avram Iancu Square, with the Orthodox Cathedral, next to the National Theatre.
In the west is the Central Park, with a lake where you can go boating in summer and skating in winter.
On a hill by the river Someș is the Cetățuia. From there you can see the whole city.
Cluj has many universities. That’s why you see students everywhere in the streets.
“să te plimbi” = to go for a walk / ride for pleasure
Someș (the river that flows through Cluj)
Cetățuia (a hill with an old fortress)
From the Cetățuia you can see the whole city.
